result.markdown: --- title: "Session 2 — Descriptive Estimates" subtitle: "svymean · svyciprop · svytotal · svyby · quantiles · design effect · subpopulations · tables · Lab 2" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: declared the design, saw why weights matter - Today: the **survey versions** of the descriptive tools you already know - By the end you can: - estimate **means, proportions, totals and quantiles** with CIs - estimate by **groups** - read a **design effect** - do a **subpopulation** analysis correctly - test an association in a **weighted table** ::: # Topic 1 — Means, proportions, totals {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Means and totals ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- svymean(~sbp, des); m; confint(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean SE sbp 125.75 0.5918 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % sbp 124.5872 126.9071 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} svytotal(~hypertension, des) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` total SE hypertension 82707 6028.3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Mean SBP **125.7 mmHg** (95% CI 124.6 to 126.9). About **82,700 adults** in the population have hypertension (SE 6,000): a **total** needs the weights, since it scales up to the population. ::: ## A proportion with a good CI ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svyciprop(~I(hypertension == 1), des, method = "logit") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 97.5% I(hypertension == 1) 0.200 0.171 0.231 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Logit** (or Wilson-type) intervals stay between 0 and 1 and behave better for small or large proportions - **20.0%**, 95% CI **17.1% to 23.1%** - Note the **`I(... == 1)`**: `svyciprop` needs a logical or 0/1 formula ::: ## By groups ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svyby(~hypertension, ~residence, des, svymean) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` residence hypertension se Rural Rural 0.1613439 0.01949068 Urban Urban 0.2969588 0.01697648 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svyby(~hypertension, ~region, des, svymean, vartype = c("se", "ci")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` region hypertension se ci_l ci_u East East 0.1893173 0.03467795 0.1213497 0.2572848 North North 0.1901994 0.02055287 0.1499165 0.2304823 South South 0.2323492 0.03664345 0.1605294 0.3041690 West West 0.1862430 0.02411113 0.1389861 0.2335000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **Urban 29.7%** vs **rural 16.1%**. Regions look alike (19 to 23%); the CIs are wide because each region has only **12 PSUs**. ::: ## Quantiles ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svyquantile(~sbp, des, quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $sbp quantile ci.2.5 ci.97.5 se 0.25 115 114 117 0.7421791 0.5 126 126 128 0.4947861 0.75 137 136 139 0.7421791 attr(,"hasci") [1] TRUE attr(,"class") [1] "newsvyquantile" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - `median()` and `quantile()` **ignore the weights**: they describe the **sample** - `svyquantile()` gives the **population** quartiles with CIs: median **126 mmHg** ::: # Topic 2 — Design effect and subpopulations {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Design effect ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svymean(~hypertension, des, deff = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean SE DEff hypertension 0.19955 0.01493 2.596 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.eq} DEFF = variance (actual design) / variance (simple random sample of the same size) n~eff~ = n / DEFF ::: ::: {.incremental} - DEFF **2.6**: the 1,853 respondents carry the information of about **710** independent adults - Comes from **clustering** (similar adults in a PSU) and **unequal weights** - **Differs by outcome**: large when the outcome varies a lot between PSUs ::: ## Subpopulations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} des_w30 <- subset(des, sex == "Female" & age >= 30) svymean(~hypertension, des_w30) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean SE hypertension 0.2174 0.0211 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Use **`subset()` on the design**, not `filter()` on the data followed by a new `svydesign()`. `subset()` keeps the **whole design** (all strata and PSUs), so the variance is right. Filtering can remove a PSU from a stratum and make the variance **wrong** or impossible. ::: ## Weighted tables and tests ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svytable(~education + hypertension, des) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` hypertension education 0 1 None 93378 25278 Primary 117640 33232 Secondary+ 120752 24197 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} svychisq(~education + hypertension, des) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's X^2: Rao & Scott adjustment data: svychisq(~education + hypertension, des) F = 3.2419, ndf = 1.8964, ddf = 75.8576, p-value = 0.04709 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Counts are **estimated numbers of adults**, not respondents - About **21% and 22%** (none, primary) vs **17%** (secondary or more) - **Rao-Scott** test (p ≈ 0.05); never `chisq.test()` on survey data ::: ## The same with srvyr (tidy syntax) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resp |> as_survey_design(ids = psu, strata = stratum, weights = weight, nest = TRUE) |> group_by(residence) |> summarise(prev = survey_mean(hypertension, vartype = "ci"), n = unweighted(n())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 residence prev prev_low prev_upp n 1 Rural 0.161 0.122 0.201 970 2 Urban 0.297 0.263 0.331 883 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} `survey_mean()`, `survey_total()`, `survey_quantile()` plug into `group_by()` and `summarise()`; `unweighted(n())` gives the **respondent** count. ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 2 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `survey-workshop/labs/lab2_describe.R` - means, proportions with logit CI, totals - `svyby`, quantiles and the design effect - subpopulation, weighted table and srvyr ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v2q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="b87rkd.29zmly" data-show="SXQga2VlcHMgdGhlIGludGVydmFsIGJldHdlZW4gMCBhbmQgMSBhbmQgc3VpdHMgc21hbGwg cHJvcG9ydGlvbnM=" data-explain="QSBzeW1tZXRyaWMgaW50ZXJ2YWwgY2FuIGZhbGwgYmVsb3cgMCBvciBhYm92ZSAxIGZvciBw cm9wb3J0aW9ucyBuZWFyIHRoZSBlbmRzLiBUaGUgbG9naXQgc2NhbGUga2VlcHMgbGltaXRz IGluc2lkZSB0aGUgcmFuZ2Uu"} Why is the logit method often chosen for the CI of a prevalence? - It makes the interval narrower than a symmetric one around the estimate - It removes the design effect from the standard error of the proportion - It is the only method that works when weights are present - It keeps the interval between 0 and 1 and suits small proportions ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v2q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="b884sz.2a0138" data-show="VGhlIGZ1bGwgZGVzaWduIGlzIGtlcHQsIHNvIHRoZSB2YXJpYW5jZSByZWZsZWN0cyBhbGwg c3RyYXRhIGFuZCBQU1Vz" data-explain="U3VicG9wdWxhdGlvbiBlc3RpbWF0ZXMgbXVzdCB1c2UgdGhlIGNvbXBsZXRlIGRlc2lnbi4g UmVtb3Zpbmcgcm93cyBjYW4gZHJvcCBQU1VzIGFuZCBjaGFuZ2UgdGhlIHZhcmlhbmNlLCBz b21ldGltZXMgbGVhdmluZyBzdHJhdGEgd2l0aCBhIHNpbmdsZSBQU1Uu"} Why use subset() on the design instead of filtering the data and declaring the design again? - The full design is kept, so the variance reflects all strata and PSUs - Filtering rescales the weights so that they add up to the sample size - subset() is quicker because it does not need to look at the strata - Filtering removes the variable that identifies the strata from the data ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v2q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="b88i1q.2a0fkn" data-show="QWJvdXQgNzEwIHJlc3BvbmRlbnRz" data-explain="VGhlIGVmZmVjdGl2ZSBzYW1wbGUgc2l6ZSBpcyBuIGRpdmlkZWQgYnkgdGhlIGRlc2lnbiBl ZmZlY3Q6IDEsODUzIC8gMi42IGlzIGFib3V0IDcxMC4="} The design effect for hypertension is 2.6 and n is 1,853. What is the effective sample size? - About 4,800 respondents - About 1,850 respondents - About 710 respondents - About 70 respondents ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v2q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="b88vae.2a0u1z" data-show="VGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBhZHVsdHMgaW4gdGhlIHBvcHVsYXRpb24gd2hvIGhhdmUgaHlwZXJ0 ZW5zaW9u" data-explain="QSB0b3RhbCBpcyB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0ZWQgc3VtOiBlYWNoIHJlc3BvbmRlbnQgY291bnRzIGZv ciB0aGUgbnVtYmVyIG9mIGFkdWx0cyBoZSBvciBzaGUgcmVwcmVzZW50cywgZ2l2aW5nIGEg cG9wdWxhdGlvbiBjb3VudC4="} svytotal(~hypertension, des) gives 82,700. What does this estimate? - The number of respondents in the sample who have hypertension - The number of adults in the population who have hypertension - The mean blood pressure of the adults who have hypertension - The number of PSUs in which hypertension was recorded ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v2q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="b898j4.2a18jd" data-show="bWVkaWFuKCkgaWdub3JlcyB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0cywgc28gaXQgZGVzY3JpYmVzIHRoZSBzYW1w bGU=" data-explain="VGhlIG9yZGluYXJ5IG1lZGlhbiB0cmVhdHMgZXZlcnkgcmVzcG9uZGVudCBlcXVhbGx5LiBU aGUgc3VydmV5IHZlcnNpb24gYXBwbGllcyB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0cywgc28gaXQgZXN0aW1hdGVz IHRoZSBwb3B1bGF0aW9uIG1lZGlhbi4="} Why should svyquantile() be used rather than median() for the median SBP of the population? - median() cannot handle missing values in the blood pressure column - svyquantile() is for percentages while median() is for means - median() ignores the weights, so it describes the sample - median() needs the data to be sorted by stratum before it is called ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - `svymean`, `svytotal`, `svyciprop(method = "logit")`, `svyquantile`, `svyby` - **DEFF** = variance ratio; **n~eff~ = n / DEFF** - **`subset(design)`**, never filter then re-declare - `svytable` + **Rao-Scott** (`svychisq`), not `chisq.test()` - srvyr: `as_survey_design()` + `survey_mean()` ::: **Next:** Session 3: regression with survey data

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
